lines: A threshold shaper on the positive side of a signal: once the input plus BIAS rises past SET, the sample is replaced by the level AMT sets, and below that it passes straight through
Adds 0 to 5V to the input before it is compared with SET, and reaches the output no other way
Sets the level, 0 to 10V, that the input plus BIAS has to pass for the sample to be replaced
Sets the level a passing sample is replaced by, 0V fully left to 6V fully right
The signal to be processed, of which only the first channel is read
Replaces the SET knob with this voltage for as long as it is patched
Replaces the AMT knob for as long as it is patched: the size of the voltage, divided by 10 and multiplied by 6, becomes the replacement level
Replaces the BIAS knob with this voltage for as long as it is patched
The processed signal, always one channel
Note — each of the three CV jacks replaces its knob outright rather than adding to it, so patching one takes that knob out of use entirely
Note — only the positive side is treated: a sample whose total stays below the threshold passes through untouched, and the negative half of a waveform is never touched at all
Note — with AMT at zero a passing sample is set to 0.1V rather than to zero
Note — the module browser calls this a wavefolder, but the code replaces the sample with a level rather than reflecting it back, so what comes out is a flat step rather than a fold

Pleats.notes: The folding arithmetic reduces to a replacement rather than a fold: Pleats.cpp:92-103 computes delta as the sample minus the fold amount and then subtracts delta from the sample, which leaves the fold amount itself. The maker's own comment on line 104 asks what about the negative half, and nothing in the code treats it. The Amount CV jack takes the absolute value of its voltage, so it cannot drive the level below zero.

lines: A chaotic CV source: a Henon or Ikeda attractor stepped forward at a rate you set or at an external clock, with its two coordinates on the outputs and a gate for every step
Sets how often a new value is taken, on a logarithmic scale from one every 20 seconds fully left to 500 a second fully right; it is ignored while CLOCK is patched
Adds -2V to +2V to both CV outputs
Sets how much of each step the gate output stays high, from a thousandth of it to all of it
Chooses which attractor is stepped: Henon or Ikeda
Sets the constant the attractor is built on, mapped to between 0.7 and 1.0, which changes the run of values it produces
Takes the tempo from the time between two rising edges past 2V, one new value to the beat, and takes over from RATE
10V for the fraction of each step set by GATE and 0V for the rest of it
The attractor's first coordinate with BIAS added, held at that value until the next step
The attractor's second coordinate with BIAS added, held at that value until the next step
Note — in Ikeda mode the step rate also follows the attractor's own magnitude, so the steps come unevenly; in Henon mode that term is one and the rate is steady
Note — the attractor is put back to its starting point whenever a coordinate reaches -2.2V in Henon mode or -2V in Ikeda mode, which is what stops it sticking
Note — all three outputs are one channel, and the two CV outputs hold their value between steps

Strange.notes: With no clock patched the step length is ten to the power of minus the Rate knob, multiplied by the squared modulus of the Ikeda value and by a fifth of the sample rate (Strange.cpp:116). In Henon mode that modulus is held at one, so the rate is steady; in Ikeda mode it moves with the attractor. The two CV outputs are the raw attractor coordinates with the bias added and are not clamped, so their range depends on the attractor rather than on any setting.

Trip.notes: Trip.cpp:288-290 returns from process as soon as it finds the clock jack unconnected, so without a clock nothing at all is written. The bar count passed to spaceScale is not used by it (Trip.cpp:589-601): the button normalises the eight time-share knobs to a total of one whatever the bar count says, and the count is applied separately when each step's length is worked out. The automatic reduction of the octave setting only inspects steps whose time share is above zero, so with every share at zero the octave is left alone and the CV outputs can reach 9V.

lines: A sine oscillator built on a two-state recurrence, with two outputs a quarter cycle apart and one control that pushes the tone towards harmonics and aliasing
Adds a fixed amount to the oscillator's running state every sample, 0 to 2, which bends the sine towards harmonics and aliasing; with the ALIASING jack patched it scales that voltage instead
Drives the shape amount from a voltage, a fifth of it multiplied by half the SHAPE knob, so the knob has to be off zero for this jack to do anything
Sets the pitch at 1V per octave, with 0V giving C4 at 261.63Hz
The main output, five times the sine of the running state
The quadrature output, five times the sine of the other state, a quarter cycle from the main one
Note — no pitch input is needed: with nothing patched to V/OCT the oscillator runs at C4
Note — the oscillator resets its own state whenever the pitch changes at all, so a continuously moving V/OCT holds it at a standstill rather than sweeping it
Note — both outputs are one channel

Smitty.notes: Smitty.cpp:57-61 resets the oscillator state and sets epsilon to zero on any change of frequency, so while a V/OCT input is moving the module outputs five times the sine of a constant rather than a swept tone; it settles as soon as the pitch is held. With the shape CV patched the knob acts as its attenuator, so at a knob setting of zero the jack has no effect at all.
